notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Thessalonians 1. I've included only what the pages I read actually say. A few gaps first:

- **Missing sources:** I couldn't reach NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, OCA, catholic.com, or any Lutheran site (lcms.org, 1517.org).
- **No popular-teaching material:** nothing turned up on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Thin on vv. 8–10:** I had only part of Chrysostom (Homily 1, which covers vv. 1–6) and a short preview of Sam Storms' sermon.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul usually worked with a team when he could, and he names his co-workers here. He likely wrote this from Corinth after Silas and Timothy brought good news, probably his first letter to any church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Guzik, quoting Hiebert: putting "God the Father" and "the Lord Jesus Christ" under one preposition ("in") places the two names side by side on a basis of equality. It is a clear witness to his conviction concerning the deity of Jesus Christ. Morris also notes the shift from the usual Greek letter greeting (*chairein*) to "grace" (*charis*). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Wesley (Methodist): Paul uses no title, not even "apostle," because he is writing very familiarly to sincere, simple-hearted people. He also says the letter has a sweetness free of rebuke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
- Chrysostom (Catholic/Orthodox Church Father): Paul skips his title because these converts were new and had no experience of him yet. He calls them "church" to encourage a group that was probably small and not yet organised. Being "in God" is a dignity with no equal, and Chrysostom warns that someone enslaved to sin cannot be said to be in God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230401.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik, citing Hiebert: the present tense suggests thanks given regularly, never skipping a day. Paul was thankful even though the church was planted after only about three weekends (Acts 17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Chrysostom: thanking God for them, not just praising them, credits God with doing it all and teaches them humility. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230401.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik, citing Hiebert: this is the first time, chronologically, that Paul uses the triad of faith, love and hope. His stress falls on what each produces: work, labour and endurance. Paul was not thankful because the church was flawless; he later corrects their doctrine and sexual conduct. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Wesley: faith is "active, ever-working," and love is continually labouring for people's bodies or souls. Faith works, love labours, hope patiently suffers all things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
- Chrysostom: the "work of faith" is steadfastness that nothing could turn aside. Merely loving is no labour, but loving genuinely under pressure is, as with Jason risking himself for Paul (Acts 17). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230401.htm

**v. 4: the main point where traditions differ (election)**
- **Shared reading:** Paul knows they are chosen from the visible evidence described in vv. 5–10.
  - TGC: Paul's knowledge comes from how the gospel arrived and how it was received. They are "chosen" by God unto salvation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/
  - Matthew Henry: Paul had not read the records of eternity; he knew their election from the gospel's success among them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_001.cfm
  - Guzik: "beloved by God" was a phrase Jews kept for figures like Moses and Solomon, and for Israel. Here it is given to humble Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- **Reformed and Calvinist Baptist (eternal, individual, unconditional election):**
  - Gill: this is the eternal choice of them to everlasting life, an act of God the Father in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
  - Poole: election means choosing some out of others. He rejects both the idea that it is only a separation at conversion and the idea that it is conditional on perseverance, because Paul affirms their election before seeing them persevere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
  - Meyer: God predetermined individuals from eternity to be believers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
  - Henry: election comes from God's good pleasure, not from any merit in those chosen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_001.cfm
  - Spurgeon: election is sovereign, cannot be reversed, and is effective. In vv. 4–6 he finds four evidences: the Word coming with power, receiving it with assurance, following Christ, and joy. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/election-its-defences-and-evidences/
- **Methodist and Wesleyan:**
  - Wesley: election is through faith, by these plain proofs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
  - Adam Clarke: the election here is God calling Gentiles to the privileges once given to the Jews. No irrespective, unconditional, eternal, and personal election to everlasting glory, is meant by the apostle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-thessalonians-1.html
  - Barnes, a Presbyterian commentator, rejects Clarke's reading: the church included many Jews, and choosing groups instead of individuals leaves the same difficulties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
- **Holiness:** Godbey teaches that election comes through "sanctification of the Spirit." In conversion we become candidates for heaven; in sanctification we are elected. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsb/1-thessalonians/1-9.html
- **Lutheran pietist:** The Biblical Illustrator quotes Bengel (a Lutheran). Bengel holds that everyone called is elect from the first moment of faith, but whoever loses calling and faith "ceases to be elected." The same source reads the election here as of a people, not individuals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-3.html
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** in Paul and Peter, election mainly means being let into religious privileges in this life. It implies nothing about the person's final state. https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
  - The Bible Hub commentary page also says that all baptised persons are elect but may unsettle their election or make it sure. That excerpt didn't name the commentator, so I can't confirm who said it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-4.htm
- **Charismatic Reformed (Sam Storms):** Paul claims to know they are elect only after they believed, once their lives showed the evidence. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/chosen-by-god-and-delivered-from-wrath-1-thessalonians-1:1-10

**v. 5**
- Expositor's Bible: verse 5 explains how Paul knows they are elect, not what election is. Part of the evidence lay in the preachers themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-thessalonians-1.html
- **Who had the "full conviction"?** Precept Austin notes there is no consensus. Hiebert and the Amplified Bible take it as the missionaries' own conviction. The NLT takes it as assurance given to the Thessalonians. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59599
- **Wesleyan reading (power and the Spirit):**
  - Wesley: "power" means piercing the heart with a sense of sin, and "the Holy Ghost" includes outward testimony by miracles. The extraordinary works of the Spirit are never wholly withheld where the gospel is preached with power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
  - Clarke: the Spirit gave them full assurance both that the gospel was true and that their sins were forgiven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-thessalonians-1.html
- **Reformed and Baptist reading:**
  - Henry: unless the Spirit comes with the Word, it is a dead letter. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_001.cfm
  - Spurgeon: The Gospel is preached in the ears of all; it only comes with power to some. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/election-its-defences-and-evidences/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Paul was not shy about saying "follow me," which shows personal discipleship. Their joy under affliction echoes Paul and Silas singing in the Philippian jail. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Precept Austin: the Thessalonians became third-generation imitators: Christ first, Paul second, then them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59599
- Chrysostom: the affliction was in bodily things and the joy in spiritual ones. Like the three young men refreshed in the furnace, the Spirit refreshed them in their sufferings. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230401.htm
- Expositor's Bible: this mix of affliction and spiritual joy is the token of election. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-thessalonians-1.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Paul was an example to them, and they became examples to others. That is how God's work should spread. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: "sounded forth" suggests a ringing sound like a trumpet blast. Spreading the gospel needs both the spoken word and visible faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Wesley: the word echoed out from Thessalonica partly because it was a great commercial city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
- Chrysostom, in his homilies on Romans, cites this verse: the disciples had become teachers, and the preaching spread "more rapidly than fire." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210202.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: their changed lives were so visible that others could see and talk about the change without Paul explaining it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-1/
- Wesley: "they themselves" means the people wherever the missionaries went. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm

**v. 10: the second point where views differ (what is "the coming wrath"?)**
- **Shared points:**
  - Pulpit Commentary: "delivers" is a present participle. The deliverance began with Christ's death but will not be complete until his return. https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/1-10.htm
  - Wesley: He redeemed us once; he delivers us continually, and he will deliver believers from eternal vengeance. He reads the resurrection as proof that Christ will come to judge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_thessalonians/1.htm
  - Constable: every chapter of this letter ends with a reference to Christ's return. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
- **Final judgment, general:**
  - Barnes: the wrath is God's indignation on the guilty, from which Christ saves by dying in our place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/1-10.htm
  - Coffman: it refers to the judgment of the Great Day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
  - Sam Storms: it is wrath on the day of judgment, from which only Jesus delivers, since he endured it himself. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/chosen-by-god-and-delivered-from-wrath-1-thessalonians-1:1-10
- **Pre-tribulation (dispensational) reading:**
  - Fruchtenbaum, quoted by Precept Austin: believers are already redeemed from hell, so this must be the wrath of the Great Tribulation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_thessalonians_110
  - Precept Austin itself admits no single verse proves a pre-tribulation rapture, but sees a strong hint of one here. It notes MacArthur instead reads the verse as rescue from eternal judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_thessalonians_110
  - Bible.org lists this verse as an argument for a pre-tribulation rapture and for "imminence" (Christ could return at any time). https://bible.org/article/rapture-debate
  - Constable: taken alone, the verse would most likely mean wrath on unbelievers in general, but the wider biblical teaching points to a pre-tribulation rapture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) allows either eternal punishment or the tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
- **Historical readings:** Clarke includes the coming destruction of the unbelieving Jews. Gann mentions the AD 70 tribulation as a possibility. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
- **Assurance (Spurgeon):** It is presumption to live without knowing that you are delivered from wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/1-10.html
